claim: Frontal motor areas are central to controlling voluntary movements.
source: Frontal motor areas are central to controlling voluntary movements.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about frontal motor areas.

claim: In non-human primates, the motor areas contain independent, somatotopic, representations of the forelimb (i.e., motor maps).
source: In non-human primates, the motor areas contain independent, somatotopic, representations of the forelimb (i.e., motor maps).
evidence: This statement references established knowledge about motor area organization in non-human primates.

claim: Two macaque monkeys performed an instructed reach-to-grasp task while cortical activity was recorded with intrinsic signal optical imaging (ISOI).
source: Two macaque monkeys performed an instructed reach-to-grasp task while cortical activity was recorded with intrinsic signal optical imaging (ISOI).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: The spatial extent of activity in M1 and PMd was quantified in relation to the forelimb motor maps, which were obtained from the same hemisphere with intracortical microstimulation.
source: The spatial extent of activity in M1 and PMd was then quantified in relation to the forelimb motor maps, which we obtained from the same hemisphere with intracortical microstimulation.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach for quantifying cortical activity.

claim: ISOI showed that task-related activity was concentrated in patches that collectively overlapped <40% of the M1 and PMd forelimb representations.
source: ISOI showed that task-related activity was concentrated in patches that collectively overlapped <40% of the M1 and PMd forelimb representations.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the ISOI measurements reported in the study.

claim: The spatial organization of the patches was consistent across task conditions despite small variations in forelimb use.
source: The spatial organization of the patches was consistent across task conditions despite small variations in forelimb use.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing activity patterns across different task conditions.

claim: The largest condition differences in forelimb use were reflected in the magnitude of cortical activity.
source: Nevertheless, the largest condition differences in forelimb use were reflected in the magnitude of cortical activity.
evidence: This describes a relationship between behavioral measurements and cortical activity magnitude.

claim: Distinct time course profiles from patches in arm zones and patches in hand zones suggest functional differences within the forelimb representations.
source: Distinct time course profiles from patches in arm zones and patches in hand zones suggest functional differences within the forelimb representations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of temporal differences observed in the ISOI data from different somatotopic zones.

claim: The forelimb representations contain subzones enriched with neurons tuned for specific actions.
source: The results collectively support an organizational framework wherein the forelimb representations contain subzones enriched with neurons tuned for specific actions.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the collective results of the study.

claim: The spatial dimension of neural activity appears to be an important organizing feature of the neural code in frontal motor areas.
source: Thus, the often-overlooked spatial dimension of neural activity appears to be an important organizing feature of the neural code in frontal motor areas.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spatial organization patterns observed in the study.

claim: Both M1 and PMd cortical areas contain complete motor representations of the forelimb.
source: Both cortical areas contain complete motor representations of the forelimb (e.g., Boudrias et al., 2010; Gould et al., 1986; Murphy et al., 1978; Raos et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Somatotopy of the forelimb representations varies across studies, but there is consensus that muscles and cortical columns do not have a one-to-one mapping.
source: Somatotopy of the forelimb representations varies across studies, but there is consensus that muscles and cortical columns do not have a one-to-one mapping.
evidence: This statement references established knowledge from the literature.

claim: An arm or a hand muscle receives corticospinal inputs from a population of cortical columns.
source: Instead, an arm or a hand muscle receives corticospinal inputs from a population of cortical columns (Andersen et al., 1975; Rathelot and Strick, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A cortical column can influence activity in several muscles.
source: Similarly, a cortical column can influence activity in several muscles (Donoghue et al., 1992; Fetz and Cheney, 1980; Lemon et al., 1987).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The convergence and divergence of corticospinal projections mean that the same motor output is present in many locations within a forelimb representation.
source: The convergence and divergence of corticospinal projections mean that the same motor output is present in many locations within a forelimb representation.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the convergence and divergence patterns described.

claim: Intracortical microstimulation (ICMS) evokes shoulder flexion from many M1 sites where the affiliate corticospinal projections target the same group of arm muscles.
source: For example, intracortical microstimulation (ICMS) evokes shoulder flexion from many M1 sites where the affiliate corticospinal projections target the same group of arm muscles (Park et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Electrophysiological studies examining relationships between neural coding, recording site location, and forelimb behavior support the view that neural codes for arm and hand actions are not spatially organized within the forelimb motor maps.
source: This scheme has support in electrophysiological studies that examined relationships between neural coding, recording site location, and forelimb behavior (Rouse and Schieber, 2016; Saleh et al., 2012; Vargas-Irwin et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Most electrophysiological investigations pool results across recording sites, offering only limited insight into the spatial organization of functions.
source: Nevertheless, most electrophysiological investigations pool results across recording sites, offering only limited insight into the spatial organization of functions.
evidence: This is a critical observation about the limitations of typical electrophysiological approaches.

claim: Long train ICMS (500 ms) approximates the duration of natural actions.
source: This spatial organization of function is consistent with maps obtained using long train ICMS (500 ms), which approximates the duration of natural actions (Graziano et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Long train ICMS motor mapping parameters revealed functional subzones in both frontal and parietal cortical areas.
source: The same motor mapping parameters revealed functional subzones in both frontal and parietal cortical areas (Cooke and Graziano, 2004; Gharbawie et al., 2011; Graziano et al., 2002; Stepniewska et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ISOI, two-photon imaging, and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) have been successfully used in measuring cortical activity related to arm and hand actions in monkeys.
source: Intrinsic signal optical imaging (ISOI), two-photon imaging, and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) have been successfully used in measuring cortical activity related to arm and hand actions in monkeys (Ebina et al., 2018; Friedman et al., 2020a; Kondo et al., 2018; Nelissen and Vanduffel, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The mesoscopic field-of-view (FOV) in ISOI is particularly well suited for the size of the forelimb representations in M1 and PMd.
source: The mesoscopic field-of-view (FOV) in ISOI is particularly well suited for the size of the forelimb representations in M1 and PMd.
evidence: This is a justification for the choice of ISOI as the imaging method.

claim: ISOI affords high spatial resolution and contrast without extrinsic agents (e.g., GCaMP, dyes, or MION).
source: Moreover, ISOI affords high spatial resolution and contrast without extrinsic agents (e.g., GCaMP, dyes, or MION).
evidence: This describes an advantage of ISOI as an imaging technique.

claim: The general organization of the motor map was consistent between monkeys.
source: The general organization of the motor map was consistent between monkeys (Figure 2B–D, F–H).
evidence: This is a finding from the motor mapping data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Most ICMS sites evoked forelimb movements.
source: Most ICMS sites evoked forelimb movements (Figure 2B, F).
evidence: This is a finding from the motor mapping data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The rostral border of M1 was marked such that it was 3–5 mm from the central sulcus and separated high threshold sites (>30 μA) from low threshold sites.
source: We marked the rostral border of M1 such that (1) it was 3–5 mm from the central sulcus, and (2) separated high threshold sites (>30 μA) from low threshold sites (Figure 2C, G).
evidence: This describes the criteria used to define the M1 border in the motor maps.

claim: Within the M1 forelimb representation, the main hand zone (i.e., digits and wrist) was surrounded by an arm zone, or an arm and trunk zone.
source: Within the M1 forelimb representation, the main hand zone (i.e., digits and wrist) was surrounded by an arm zone, or an arm and trunk zone.
evidence: This describes the somatotopic organization observed in the motor maps.

claim: This nested organization is consistent with previous maps from macaque monkeys.
source: This nested organization is consistent with previous maps from macaque monkeys (Murphy et al., 1978; Sessle and Wiesendanger, 1982) including maps obtained with stimulus triggered averaging of EMG activity (Park et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement compares the current findings to previous studies.

claim: The organization of the forelimb representations was less clear in PMd and PMv, which could have been related to higher thresholds, less extensive mapping, as well as more overlap between arm and hand zones than in M1.
source: The organization of the forelimb representations was less clear in PMd and PMv, which could have been related to higher thresholds, less extensive mapping, as well as more overlap between arm and hand zones than in M1 (Boudrias et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an observation about the motor maps with speculation about potential causes.

claim: Under red illumination (630 nm wavelength), negative reflectance (i.e., pixel darkening) is a lagging indicator of increased neural activity.
source: Under red illumination (630 nm wavelength), which was used here, negative reflectance (i.e., pixel darkening) is a lagging indicator of increased neural activity (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the interpretation of ISOI signals under the specific illumination conditions used.

claim: In the movement conditions, pixels would darken in locations where neural activity increased for movement execution, movement planning, or both.
source: Thus, in the movement conditions, we assumed that pixels would darken in locations where neural activity increased for movement execution, movement planning, or both.
evidence: This is an assumption about the interpretation of pixel darkening in the context of the task.

claim: During reach, grasp, and hold (+0.5 to +2.0 s from Cue), pixels in the center of the FOV brightened (cool colors).
source: During reach, grasp, and hold (+0.5 to +2.0 s from Cue), pixels in the center of the FOV brightened (cool colors).
evidence: This describes an observation from the ISOI time series data.

claim: In the same period, pixel darkening mostly overlapped the central sulcus and superior arcuate sulcus.
source: In the same period, pixel darkening mostly overlapped the central sulcus and superior arcuate sulcus (landmarks on first panel).
evidence: This describes an observation from the ISOI time series data.

claim: Pixel darkening in the period from +0.5 to +2.0 s from Cue is interpreted as indication of activity in major vessels.
source: For now, however, we interpret pixel darkening in this period as indication of activity in major vessels.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed pixel darkening pattern.

claim: Once the hand returned to the start position after movement completion (i.e., hold start), pixels in the center of the FOV started to darken and form patches in M1 and PMd (+3.5 s from Cue).
source: Once the hand returned to the start position after movement completion (i.e., hold start), we observed the expected reflectance change: pixels in the center of the FOV started to darken and form patches in M1 and PMd (+3.5 s from Cue).
evidence: This describes an observation from the ISOI time series data.

claim: Patches continued to darken and expand in the remaining frames.
source: Patches continued to darken and expand in the remaining frames.
evidence: This describes the temporal evolution of the patches observed in ISOI.

claim: Even at peak intensity and size (+5.0 to +6.0 s from Cue), patches remained spatially separable within M1 and between M1 and PMd.
source: Nevertheless, even at peak intensity and size (+5.0 to +6.0 s from Cue), patches remained spatially separable within M1 and between M1 and PMd.
evidence: This describes the spatial organization of patches at their peak.

claim: In the withhold condition, pixel darkening was limited to major blood vessels as most of the FOV was unchanged or brightened.
source: Here, pixel darkening was limited to major blood vessels as most of the FOV was unchanged or brightened (Figure 3B, cyan pixels).
evidence: This describes the ISOI response in the withhold condition shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The patches in the power grip condition were likely lagging indicators of movement-related neural activity.
source: Thus, the patches in Figure 3A were likely lagging indicators of movement-related neural activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the contrast between movement and withhold conditions.

claim: Red pixels in thresholded maps show locations of movement-related neural activity from a single session.
source: Thus, red pixels in Figure 3G show locations of movement-related neural activity from a single session.
evidence: This describes the interpretation of the thresholded map in Figure 3G.

claim: The small number of zones and their small size in the withhold condition indicates that reflectance change was limited in the absence of movement.
source: The small number of zones and their small size indicates that reflectance change was limited in the absence of movement.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the thresholded map from the withhold condition.

claim: For the arm ROIs, positive reflectance started to increase ~0.3 s after movement onset (+0.8 s from Cue) and peaked during the hold phase (+1.7 s from Cue).
source: For the arm ROIs, positive reflectance started to increase ~0.3 s after movement onset (+0.8 s from Cue) and peaked during the hold phase (+1.7 s from Cue) when the object was grasped and maintained in the lifted position.
evidence: This describes the time course of reflectance change in arm ROIs.

claim: For the arm ROIs, negative reflectance increased and peaked 2–3 s after movement completion (+5.0 to +6.0 s from Cue).
source: Then, negative reflectance increased and peaked 2–3 s after movement completion (+5.0 to +6.0 s from Cue).
evidence: This describes the time course of reflectance change in arm ROIs.

claim: The time course of the hand ROI did not show the positive reflectance that lasted for several seconds in the arm ROIs.
source: In contrast, the time course of the hand ROI did not show the positive reflectance that lasted for several seconds in the arm ROIs.
evidence: This describes a difference between hand and arm ROI time courses.

claim: The distinctiveness of the time courses from the arm and hand may reflect functional differences between those zones.
source: The distinctiveness of the time courses from the arm and hand may reflect functional differences between those zones.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed time course differences.

claim: The same ROIs showed no reflectance change in the withhold condition.
source: In contrast to the profiles in Figure 3I, the same ROIs showed no reflectance change in the withhold condition (Figure 3J).
evidence: This describes the control condition results shown in Figure 3J.

claim: In no-go trials, movements were truncated but not inhibited.
source: Movements in no-go trials were therefore truncated but not inhibited.
evidence: This describes the behavioral outcome in no-go trials.

claim: In the movement condition, the thresholded map showed patches of activity in post-movement frames as compared to baseline frames.
source: In the movement condition, the thresholded map showed patches of activity in post-movement frames as compared to baseline frames (Figure 3K, t-test, p < 0.0001).
evidence: This describes the results shown in Figure 3K.

claim: The thresholded map from the no-go condition had fewer and smaller patches than the movement condition.
source: In contrast, the thresholded map from the no-go condition had fewer and smaller patches (Figure 3L).
evidence: This describes the results shown in Figure 3L.

claim: Experiment 1 shows that significant pixel darkening was contingent on movement execution.
source: Experiment 1 therefore shows that significant pixel darkening was contingent on movement execution.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the no-go experiment results.

claim: In M1, time courses had a clear negative peak in the performed trials but remained near baseline in the observed trials.
source: In M1, time courses had a clear negative peak in the performed trials (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) but remained near baseline in the observed trials.
evidence: This describes the results from Experiment 2 shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In PMd, the performed and observed trials had overlapping time courses.
source: In PMd however, the performed and observed trials had overlapping time courses.
evidence: This describes the results from Experiment 2.

claim: All negative peaks in PMd were smaller than the M1 peaks in the performed trials.
source: All negative peaks in PMd were smaller than the M1 peaks in the performed trials.
evidence: This describes a quantitative comparison between M1 and PMd responses.

claim: Results from Experiment 2 suggest that M1 activity was driven by movement execution, whereas PMd activity was likely related to movement execution, movement preparation, and motor cognition.
source: Results from Experiment 2 suggest that M1 activity was driven by movement execution, whereas PMd activity was likely related to movement execution, movement preparation, and motor cognition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the differences between M1 and PMd responses in the observation experiment.

claim: Time courses from both monkeys confirmed that the negative peaks were locked to Cue onset, and by extension movement onset.
source: Time courses from both monkeys confirmed that the negative peaks were locked to Cue onset, and by extension movement onset.
evidence: This describes the results from Experiment 3 shown in Figure 4.

claim: Experiment 3 shows that peak map size, and the timing of the negative peak, were both locked to movement onset.
source: Thus, Experiment 3 shows that peak map size, and the timing of the negative peak, were both locked to movement onset.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results of Experiment 3.

claim: Experiments 1–3 confirm that the M1 activity reported here was linked to movement execution, whereas PMd activity was likely more complex.
source: Collectively, Experiments 1–3 confirm that the M1 activity reported here was linked to movement execution, whereas PMd activity was likely more complex.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the three control experiments.

claim: During movement, pixel darkening was limited to major vessels; the rest of the FOV brightened or was unchanged.
source: (1) During movement, pixel darkening was limited to major vessels; the rest of the FOV brightened or was unchanged.
evidence: This describes a spatiotemporal feature observed in the average time series.

claim: Pixel darkening in cortex (i.e., beyond major vessels) occurred after movement completion.
source: (2) Pixel darkening in cortex (i.e., beyond major vessels) occurred after movement completion.
evidence: This describes a spatiotemporal feature observed in the average time series.

claim: The intensity of pixel darkening and the number of pixels that darkened progressed gradually from movement completion until the end of image acquisition.
source: (3) The intensity of pixel darkening and the number of pixels that darkened progressed gradually from movement completion until the end of image acquisition.
evidence: This describes a spatiotemporal feature observed in the average time series.

claim: The same features were present in the other movement conditions.
source: The same features were present in the other movement conditions (not shown).
evidence: This indicates consistency of the observed features across conditions.

claim: Peak times fit into three broad categories: early peaks, intermediate peaks, and late peaks.
source: Peak times fit into three broad categories (Figure 5B). (1) Early peaks. Green pixels peaked ~2 s from Cue when the monkey was still engaged in task-related movements. Green pixels generally corresponded with the hot color pixels in Figure 5A panels 1.6–2.5, and therefore may have been affiliated with the early response in major vessels. (2) Intermediate peaks. Orange/yellow pixels peaked ~3.5 s from Cue, which was within 1 s of movement completion. Orange/yellow pixels were in the approximate location of yellow pixels in Figure 5A last panel. (3) Late peaks. Magenta/red pixels peaked ~5.5 s from Cue, which was ~3.0 s from movement completion.
evidence: This describes the categorization of peak times observed in Figure 5B.

claim: In the movement conditions, time courses from the three ROIs had motion artifact that started with reach onset (~0.5 s from Cue) and lasted for ~0.2 s.
source: In the movement conditions, time courses from the three ROIs had motion artifact that started with reach onset (Figure 5C–E; ~0.5 s from Cue) and lasted for ~0.2 s.
evidence: This describes an artifact observed in the time courses.

claim: For the M1 hand ROI, after the artifact, reflectance change was flat for ~1.5 s.
source: For the M1 hand ROI (Figure 5C), after the artifact, reflectance change was flat for ~1.5 s.
evidence: This describes the time course from the M1 hand ROI.

claim: Negative reflectance started to increase ~2.5 s from Cue, which coincided with the end of movement in the precision and power conditions.
source: Negative reflectance started to increase ~2.5 s from Cue, which coincided with the end of movement in the precision and power conditions.
evidence: This describes the timing of negative reflectance increase in relation to movement.

claim: In the precision and power conditions, the negative peak was larger, and occurred later, than in the reach-only condition.
source: In those conditions, the negative peak was larger, and occurred later, than in the reach-only condition.
evidence: This describes a comparison of negative peaks across conditions.

claim: ROIs in M1 and PMd arm zones returned time courses that were consistent with one another.
source: ROIs in M1 and PMd arm zones returned time courses that were consistent with one another (Figure 5D, E).
evidence: This describes the similarity between arm zone time courses.

claim: In both arm ROIs, the motion artifact was followed by an increase in positive reflectance, which is quite different from the time courses from the hand ROI.
source: In both ROIs, the motion artifact was followed by an increase in positive reflectance, which is quite different from the time courses from the hand ROI (Figure 5C).
evidence: This describes a difference between arm and hand ROI time courses.

claim: In all ROIs, the withhold condition had time courses that remained close to baseline.
source: First, in all ROIs, the withhold condition had time courses that remained close to baseline (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This describes the control condition results.

claim: The withhold condition control confirms that the reflectance change in the movement conditions was movement driven.
source: This control confirms that the reflectance change in the movement conditions was movement driven.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the withhold condition results.

claim: A ROI that comprised the entire forelimb representation of M1 and PMd returned time courses that differed entirely from the other three ROIs.
source: Second, a ROI that comprised the entire forelimb representation of M1 and PMd (Figure 5B) returned time courses that differed entirely from the other three ROIs.
evidence: This describes the results from the large forelimb ROI.

claim: The forelimb ROI lacked the characteristic negative peaks observed in the smaller ROIs.
source: Most importantly, the forelimb ROI lacked the characteristic negative peaks in Figure 5C–E.
evidence: This describes a key difference between the large forelimb ROI and smaller ROIs.

claim: The forelimb ROI control confirms that time courses from movement conditions were spatially specific responses that did not generalize to the entire forelimb representation.
source: This control confirms that time courses from movement conditions were spatially specific responses that did not generalize to the entire forelimb representation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the forelimb ROI results.

claim: The general organization of the thresholded maps was more similar across conditions within an animal than for the same condition across animals.
source: The general organization of the thresholded maps was more similar across conditions within an animal than for the same condition across animals (Figure 5G, J), which is consistent with human fMRI maps of M1 finger zones (Ejaz et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes a pattern in the thresholded maps with comparison to human fMRI studies.

claim: In all thresholded maps, significant pixels were organized in patches that overlapped subzones of the M1 and PMd forelimb representations.
source: In all thresholded maps, significant pixels were organized in patches that overlapped subzones of the M1 and PMd forelimb representations.
evidence: This describes the spatial organization observed in the thresholded maps.

claim: In each map the patches collectively overlapped only 31% (median, IQR = 29–35%) of the forelimb representations.
source: In each map the patches collectively overlapped only 31% (median, IQR = 29–35%) of the forelimb representations (Figure 5H, K).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of the spatial extent of patches.

claim: Thresholded maps from the withhold condition overlapped 3% (median, IQR = 1–7%) of the M1 and PMd forelimb representations.
source: For reference, thresholded maps from the withhold condition overlapped 3% (median, IQR = 1–7%) of the M1 and PMd forelimb representations.
evidence: This provides a control measurement for comparison.

claim: Re-thresholding the maps to correct for multiple comparisons (t-test, p < 1e−7) shrank their sizes to 14% (median, IQR = 16–20%) overlap with the forelimb representations.
source: This more conservative threshold did not impact the spatial organization of the maps, but it shrank their sizes to 14% (median, IQR = 16–20%) overlap with the forelimb representations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the effect of a more conservative statistical threshold.

claim: Expanding the frame range of thresholded maps to the 39 frames post-movement (t-test, p < 0.0001) led to only a small reduction of overlap with the forelimb representations (median = 27%, IQR = 25–34%).
source: In contrast, expanding the frame range of thresholded maps to the 39 frames post-movement (t-test, p < 0.0001) led to only a small reduction of overlap with the forelimb representations (Figure 5—figure supplement 2; median = 27%, IQR = 25–34%).
evidence: This describes the effect of using a different frame range for thresholding.

claim: Generating thresholded maps using a less conservative threshold, or using different frame ranges from the post-movement period, returned the same overall result: <40% overlap with the M1 and PMd forelimb representations.
source: Thus, generating thresholded maps using a less conservative threshold, or using different frame ranges from the post-movement period, returned the same overall result: <40% overlap with the M1 and PMd forelimb representations.
evidence: This is a summary of the robustness of the main finding across different analysis parameters.

claim: A consistent feature across movement conditions, cortical areas, and monkeys, was that the size of thresholded maps started to rapidly increase from ~3 s after Cue, which nearly coincided with the end of movement in the precision and power conditions.
source: A consistent feature across movement conditions, cortical areas, and monkeys, was that the size of thresholded maps started to rapidly increase from ~3 s after Cue, which nearly coincided with the end of movement in the precision and power conditions.
evidence: This describes a temporal pattern in the development of thresholded maps.

claim: The size of the maps plateaued, or even decreased, by ~5 s from Cue.
source: The size of the maps plateaued, or even decreased, by ~5 s from Cue.
evidence: This describes the temporal evolution of map size.

claim: At peak map expansion, overlap with the forelimb representations was 38% (median, IQR = 35–44%).
source: At peak map expansion, overlap with the forelimb representations was 38% (median, IQR = 35–44%).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of peak map size.

claim: The two strategies adopted for selecting movement frames (5- and 39-frame averages) did not underreport the size of the thresholded maps.
source: Thus, the two strategies that we adopted for selecting movement frames (5- and 39-frame averages) did not underreport the size of the thresholded maps.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the validity of the analysis approach.

claim: Time courses and non-binarized average maps showed greater magnitudes of activity in the reach-to-grasp conditions as compared to the reach-only condition.
source: Nevertheless, time courses (Figure 5C–E) and non-binarized average maps (Figure 6A) showed greater magnitudes of activity in the reach-to-grasp conditions as compared to the reach-only condition.
evidence: This describes a difference in activity magnitude across conditions.

claim: Several patches in the M1 and PMd forelimb representations darkened more in the reach-to-grasp conditions as compared to the reach-only condition.
source: After relaxing the threshold to p < 0.001, we found several patches in the M1 and PMd forelimb representations that darkened more in the reach-to-grasp conditions as compared to the reach-only condition (Figure 6B, C).
evidence: This describes the results of paired comparisons between conditions.

claim: Fewer and smaller patches reported differences between the precision and power conditions.
source: In contrast, fewer and smaller patches reported differences between the precision and power conditions (not shown).
evidence: This describes the results of paired comparisons between conditions.

claim: A one-way ANOVA showed an effect of condition pairs on the correlation coefficients (F(2,231) = 12.98, p < 0.01).
source: A one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) showed an effect of condition pairs on the correlation coefficients (F(2,231) = 12.98, p < 0.01; Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the cross-correlation analysis.

claim: Post hoc tests showed that the correlation coefficients for precision X reach-only was lower than the other two condition pairs.
source: Post hoc tests corrected for multiple comparison (n = 3; p < 0.01), showed that the correlation coefficients for precision X reach-only was lower than the other two condition pairs.
evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc testing.

claim: The cross-correlations show that the spatiotemporal patterns of cortical activity were most dissimilar between the precision and reach-only conditions.
source: The cross-correlations therefore show that the spatiotemporal patterns of cortical activity were most dissimilar between the precision and reach-only conditions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cross-correlation results.

claim: Cross-correlating movement conditions with the withhold condition returned a much lower distribution of coefficients.
source: For context, cross-correlating movement conditions with the withhold condition returned a much lower distribution of coefficients (Figure 6D).
evidence: This provides a control comparison for the cross-correlation analysis.

claim: The two approaches for directly comparing cortical activity between conditions indicate that condition differences were small but most pronounced between the precision and reach-only conditions.
source: In sum, the two approaches that we used for directly comparing cortical activity between conditions indicate that condition differences were small but most pronounced between the precision and reach-only conditions.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the condition comparison analyses.

claim: The reach-only condition stood out for having the smallest AUC in all degrees of freedom.
source: The reach-only condition stood out for having the smallest AUC (Figure 7B) in all degrees of freedom.
evidence: This describes a finding from the kinematic measurements.

claim: A one-way ANOVA detected a main effect of movement condition for AUC values of forelimb kinematic activity (F(2,4332) = 6194, p < 0.0001).
source: A one-way ANOVA detected a main effect of movement condition for AUC values of forelimb kinematic activity (F(2,4332) = 6194, p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the kinematic analysis.

claim: Post hoc tests indicated that the kinematics of forelimb joints was less for the reach-only condition than the two grasp conditions.
source: Post hoc tests corrected for multiple comparisons (n = 3; p < 0.01) indicated that the kinematics of forelimb joints was less for the reach-only condition than the two grasp conditions.
evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc testing of kinematic data.

claim: The kinematics of forelimb joints was smaller for the power condition than for the precision condition.
source: Furthurmore, the kinematics of forelimb joints was smaller for the power condition than for the precision condition.
evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc testing of kinematic data.

claim: The same condition differences in joint activity were evident in the activity of individual arm and hand muscles.
source: The same condition differences in joint activity were evident in the activity of individual arm and hand muscles (Figure 7B).
evidence: This describes consistency between kinematic and EMG measurements.

claim: A one-way ANOVA on muscle AUC measurements found a main effect (F(2,9794) = 3633, p < 0.0001).
